evidence: Suet. Gram. 23: erīlem fīlium in scholās (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: With the accusative; classical, but most frequent after the Augustan period (Lewis & Short). “Accompanied by” is the ablative absolute: magnā comitante catervā (Verg. A. 2.40), or with the noun comes, asellō comite (Phaedr. 1.11.3). “Go with someone” is also simply cum aliquō īre (see with).

terms.gloss: go along with, see off, escort
evidence: Plaut. Cas. 4.2.3: novum marītum volō rūs prōsequī (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Following someone out as an escort or in his honour: seeing him off, attending a funeral (exsequiās prōsequī). It also means to pursue an enemy, and to honour someone with words or gifts (Lewis & Short).

“A term of common life” (Lewis & Short): to escort a person out of his house as a mark of respect or for protection; redūcere is to see him home again. Its general sense is “lead away, bring down”; of a bride, to bring her to her husband’s house.

phrases.latin: vēnārī asellō comite cum vellet leō
phrases.english: when the lion wanted to go hunting with the donkey for company

phrases.latin: quīn et adultōs diū comitantur magnā ergā partum cāritāte
phrases.english: indeed they stay with their young long after they are grown, so great is their love for their offspring

phrases.latin: haec enim ipsa sunt honōrābilia quae videntur levia atque commūnia, salūtārī, adpetī, dēcēdī, adsurgī, dēdūcī, redūcī, cōnsulī
phrases.english: for these very things that seem slight and ordinary are marks of honour: to be greeted, sought out, made way for, stood up for, escorted from home and back, consulted
